newsitem.title: USA: NBA BASKETBALL-FOUR ACTIVE COACHES MAKE LIST OF NBA'S 10 BEST.
newsitem.headline: NBA BASKETBALL-FOUR ACTIVE COACHES MAKE LIST OF NBA'S 10 BEST.

text.p: Four active coaches -- Phil Jackson, Pat Riley, Lenny Wilkens and Bill Fitch -- made the list of the 10 best coaches in NBA history released Tuesday as part of the league's 50th anniversary celebration.

The legendary Red Auerbach, Red Holzman and John Kundla also made the list, as did 1980s mainstays Jack Ramsay, Chuck Daly and Don Nelson, the only coach on the list who has not won an NBA championship.

The list was compiled through balloting by media members who regularly cover the NBA. In October, a list of the 50 greatest players was released and in January, a list of the 10 greatest teams will be revealed.

Jackson, who once played for Holzman, has a career mark of 434-163 for a .727 winning percentage, best in NBA history. He has guided the Chicago Bulls to four championships in the last six years and was named Coach of the Year last season, when the Bulls went 72-10, setting an NBA mark for wins.

Riley, currently with the Miami Heat, has compiled an 816-344 mark in 14-plus seasons. He directed the Los Angeles Lakers to four titles in the 1980s and has made four other appearances in the NBA Finals with the Lakers and New York Knicks. He was Coach of the Year in 1990 and 1993.

Wilkens, coach of the Atlanta Hawks, has the most coaching wins of all time with a mark of 1,027-858. He has coached four teams in 24 seasons and guided the Seattle SuperSonics to the title in 1979. He was Coach of the Year in 1994 and is the only person on the list of greatest coaches and players.

Fitch coaches the Los Angeles Clippers, his fifth team in 21 seasons. He has compiled the most losses in NBA history but also is fourth in wins, sporting a 991-1,009 record. He earned his only NBA title with the Boston Celtics in 1981. He won coaching honours in 1976 with Cleveland and 1980 with Boston.

Auerbach, the architect of the Celtics dynasty, was 938-479 in 20 seasons as coach, 16 of them with Boston. He directed the Celtics to nine titles, including an astounding eight in a row from 1959 to 1966.
Holzman was 696-604 in 18 seasons. His advocacy of unselfish team play transformed the New York Knicks from one of the worst teams into one of the best, winning NBA titles in 1970 and 1973.
Kundla was the creative force behind the Minneapolis Lakers, the NBA's first dynasty. He won five titles in six seasons from 1949-1954 and amassed a 423-302 mark in 11 years.

Ramsay was 864-783 in 20 years as coach. He built the Buffalo Braves (now the Clippers) from expansion team to playoff team in the early 1970s and earned his only NBA title as coach of the 1977 Portland Trail Blazers.
Daly won consecutive championships with the Detroit Pistons in 1989 and 1990. He went 564-379 in 12 seasons, which also included a stint with the New Jersey Nets.

Although Nelson never coached in the NBA Finals, he is sixth on the all-time wins list with a mark of 851-630 in 19 seasons with three teams. He is the only three-time winner of the Coach of the Year award, honoured in 1983 and 1985 with Milwaukee and 1992 with Golden State.

Overlooked in the final balloting were Alex Hannum, who won two NBA titles with different teams during Auerbach's time, K.C. Jones, who was 522-252 in 10 seasons and won a pair of titles with Boston, and Bill Sharman, who won championships in the ABA and NBA, guiding the 1971-72 Lakers to a record 33 straight wins and their first title in Los Angeles.
